paragraphs: “Exactly. But hesitation, suspense, a struggle between belief and disbelief—that can be such torture to a conscientious man like you that it’s better to hang yourself at once. I knew you were inclined to believe in me, so I gave you a dose of disbelief by telling you that anecdote. I lead you to belief and disbelief by turns, and I have my reasons. It’s the new method. As soon as you stop believing in me completely, you’ll start assuring me to my face that I’m not a dream but real. I know you. Then I’ll have reached my goal, and it’s an honorable one. I’ll plant only a tiny seed of faith in you, and it will grow into an oak tree—and such an oak tree that, sitting in it, you’ll long to join ‘the hermits in the wilderness and the saintly women,’ because that is what you secretly long for. You’ll dine on locusts, you’ll wander off into the wilderness to save your soul!”
“So you’re working for the salvation of my soul, are you, you scoundrel?”
“One has to do some good work now and then. How bad-tempered you are!”
“Fool! Did you ever tempt those holy men who ate locusts and prayed for seventeen years in the wilderness until they were overgrown with moss?”

“My dear fellow, I’ve done nothing else. You forget the whole world and all the other worlds, and you fasten on one such saint, because he’s a very precious diamond. One such soul, you know, is sometimes worth a whole constellation. We have our own way of reckoning, you know. The conquest is priceless! And some of them, on my word, are not inferior to you in education, though you won’t believe it. They can look into such depths of belief and disbelief at the same moment that sometimes it really seems they’re a hair’s breadth from being ‘turned upside down,’ as the actor Gorbunov says.”
“Well, did you get your nose pulled?”[8]

“My dear fellow,” said the visitor in a lecturing tone, “it’s better to get off with a pulled nose than to have no nose at all. As an afflicted marquis said not long ago (he must have been treated by a specialist) in confession to his spiritual father, a Jesuit. I was present, it was simply charming. ‘Give me back my nose!’ he said, and he beat his breast. ‘My son,’ said the priest evasively, ‘everything is accomplished according to the inscrutable decrees of Providence, and what seems a misfortune sometimes leads to extraordinary, though hidden, benefits. If stern destiny has deprived you of your nose, it’s to your advantage that no one can ever pull you by your nose.’ ‘Holy father, that’s no comfort,’ cried the despairing marquis. ‘I’d be delighted to have my nose pulled every day of my life, if only it were in its proper place.’ ‘My son,’ sighs the priest, ‘you can’t expect every blessing at once. This is grumbling against Providence, which has not forgotten you even in this. If you complain the way you just did, saying you’d be glad to have your nose pulled for the rest of your life, then your wish has already been granted indirectly. When you lost your nose, you were led by the nose.’”
“Fool, how stupid!” cried Ivan.

“My dear friend, I only wanted to amuse you. But I swear that’s genuine Jesuit casuistry, and I swear it all happened word for word as I’ve told it. It happened lately and gave me a great deal of trouble. The unhappy young man shot himself that very night when he got home. I was at his side until the last moment. Those Jesuit confessionals are really my most delightful entertainment in melancholy moments. Here’s another incident that happened just the other day. A little blonde Norman girl of twenty—a buxom, unspoiled beauty that would make your mouth water—comes to an old priest. She bends down and whispers her sin through the grating. ‘Why, my daughter, have you fallen again already?’ cries the priest. ‘O Sancta Maria, what do I hear! Not the same man this time! How long is this going on? Aren’t you ashamed?’ ‘_Ah, mon père_,’ answers the sinner with tears of penitence, ‘_ça lui fait tant de plaisir, et à moi si peu de peine!_’ Imagine, such an answer! I drew back. It was the cry of nature, better than innocence itself, if you like. I absolved her sin on the spot and was turning to go, but I was forced to turn back. I heard the priest at the grating making a date with her for the evening—and he was an old man, hard as flint, yet he fell in an instant! It was nature, the truth of nature, asserting its rights! What, you’re turning up your nose again? Angry again? I don’t know how to please you—”

“Leave me alone, you’re hammering on my brain like a haunting nightmare,” Ivan moaned miserably, helpless before his apparition. “I’m sick of you, agonizingly and unbearably. I would give anything to be able to shake you off!”

“I repeat, lower your expectations, don’t demand of me ‘everything great and noble,’ and you’ll see how well we’ll get on,” said the gentleman impressively. “You’re really angry with me for not appearing to you in a red glow, with thunder and lightning and scorched wings, but showing myself in such a modest form. You’re wounded, first, in your aesthetic feelings, and second, in your pride. How could such a vulgar devil visit such a great man as you! Yes, there’s that romantic streak in you that Byelinsky so mocked. I can’t help it, young man. As I got ready to come to you, I did think, as a joke, of appearing as a retired general who had served in the Caucasus, with a star of the Lion and the Sun on my coat. But I was positively afraid to, because you’d have thrashed me for daring to pin the Lion and the Sun on my coat instead of, at the very least, the Polar Star or Sirius. And you keep saying I’m stupid, but, good heavens! I make no claim to be your equal in intelligence. Mephistopheles told Faust that he wanted evil but did only good. Well, he can say what he likes, with me it’s quite the opposite. I am perhaps the one being in all creation who loves the truth and truly wants good. I was there when the Word, Who died on the Cross, rose up into heaven bearing on His bosom the soul of the penitent thief. I heard the glad shrieks of the cherubim singing and shouting hosannah, and the thunderous rapture of the seraphim that shook heaven and all creation. And I swear to you by all that’s sacred, I longed to join the choir and shout hosannah with them all. The word had almost escaped me, had almost broken from my lips ... you know how susceptible and aesthetically impressionable I am. But common sense—oh, a most unfortunate trait in my character—kept me within bounds, and I let the moment pass! For what would have happened, I reflected, what would have happened after my hosannah? Everything on earth would have been extinguished at once and no events could have occurred. And so, solely from a sense of duty and my social position, I was forced to suppress the good moment and stick to my nasty task. Somebody else takes all the credit for what’s good, and nothing but nastiness is left for me. But I don’t envy the honor of a life of idle imposture, I’m not ambitious. Why am I, of all creatures in the world, doomed to be cursed by all decent people and even kicked? For if I put on mortal form, I’m bound to take such consequences sometimes. I know, of course, there’s a secret in it, but they won’t tell me the secret for anything, because then perhaps, seeing the meaning of it, I might bawl out hosannah, and the indispensable minus would disappear at once, and good sense would reign supreme throughout the whole world. And that, of course, would mean the end of everything, even of magazines and newspapers, for who would subscribe to them? I know that at the end of all things I shall be reconciled. I, too, shall walk my quadrillion and learn the secret. But until then I sulk, and I fulfill my destiny though it goes against the grain—that is, to ruin thousands for the sake of saving one. How many souls had to be ruined and how many honorable reputations destroyed for the sake of that one righteous man, Job, over whom they made such a fool of me in the old days! Yes, until the secret is revealed, there are two kinds of truth for me—one, their truth, up there, which I know nothing about so far, and the other my own. And there’s no knowing which will turn out the better.... Are you asleep?”
“I might well be,” Ivan groaned angrily. “All my stupid ideas—outgrown, thrashed out long ago, and flung aside like a dead carcass—you present to me as something new!”
“There’s no pleasing you! And I thought I’d fascinate you with my literary style. That hosannah in the skies wasn’t bad, was it? And then that ironical tone _à la_ Heine, eh?”
“No, I was never such a flunkey! How then could my soul beget a flunkey like you?”

“My dear fellow, I know a most charming and attractive young Russian gentleman, a young thinker and a great lover of literature and art, the author of a promising poem called _The Grand Inquisitor_. I was only thinking of him!”
“I forbid you to speak of _The Grand Inquisitor_,” cried Ivan, crimson with shame.
“And the _Geological Cataclysm_. Do you remember? Now that was a poem!”
“Hold your tongue, or I’ll kill you!”

“You’ll kill me? No, excuse me, I will speak. I came to treat myself to that pleasure. Oh, I love the dreams of my ardent young friends, quivering with eagerness for life! ‘There are new men,’ you decided last spring, when you were planning to come here, ‘they intend to destroy everything and begin with cannibalism. Stupid fellows! They didn’t ask my advice! I maintain that nothing needs to be destroyed, that we only need to destroy the idea of God in man, that’s how we have to set to work. That’s what we must begin with. Oh, blind race of men with no understanding! As soon as all men have denied God—and I believe that age, like the geological ages, will come to pass—the old conception of the universe will fall by itself, without cannibalism, and what’s more, the old morality will fall, and everything will begin anew. Men will unite to take from life all it can give, but only for joy and happiness in this present world. Man will be lifted up by a spirit of divine, Titanic pride, and the man-god will appear. From hour to hour, extending his conquest of nature without limit by his will and his science, man will feel such lofty joy in doing it that it will make up for all his old dreams of the joys of heaven. Everyone will know that he is mortal and will accept death proudly and serenely, like a god. His pride will teach him that it’s useless to complain that life lasts only a moment, and he will love his brother without needing any reward. Love will be enough only for a moment of life, but the very awareness of its brevity will intensify its fire, which now is dissipated in dreams of eternal love beyond the grave’... and so on and so on in the same style. Charming!”
Ivan sat with his eyes on the floor and his hands pressed to his ears, but he began trembling all over. The voice went on.

“The question now, my young thinker reflected, is whether such an age will ever come. If it does, everything is settled and humanity is established for ever. But because of man’s ingrained stupidity, this can’t come about for at least a thousand years. So everyone who recognizes the truth even now may legitimately arrange his life as he pleases, on the new principles. In that sense, ‘all things are lawful’ for him. What’s more, even if this age never comes, since there is in any case no God and no immortality, the new man may well become the man-god, even if he is the only one in the whole world. Promoted to his new position, he may lightheartedly overstep all the barriers of the old morality of the old slave-man, if necessary. There is no law for God. Where God stands, the place is holy. Where I stand will at once be the foremost place ... ‘all things are lawful’ and that’s the end of it! That’s all very charming; but if you want to swindle, why do you want a moral sanction for doing it? But that’s our modern Russian all over. He can’t bring himself to swindle without a moral sanction. He is so in love with truth—”

The visitor talked on, obviously carried away by his own eloquence, speaking louder and louder and looking ironically at his host. But he did not manage to finish. Ivan suddenly snatched a glass from the table and flung it at the orator.

“_Ah, mais c’est bête enfin_,” cried the latter, jumping up from the sofa and shaking the drops of tea off himself. “He remembers Luther’s inkstand! He takes me for a dream and throws glasses at a dream! Just like a woman! I suspected you were only pretending to stop up your ears.”
A loud, persistent knocking was suddenly heard at the window. Ivan jumped up from the sofa.
“Do you hear? You’d better open,” cried the visitor. “It’s your brother Alyosha with the most interesting and surprising news, I’ll bet!”
“Be quiet, deceiver! I knew it was Alyosha, I felt he was coming, and of course he hasn’t come for nothing; of course he brings ‘news,’” Ivan exclaimed frantically.
“Open, open to him. There’s a snowstorm and he’s your brother. _Monsieur sait-il le temps qu’il fait? C’est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors_.”

The knocking continued. Ivan wanted to rush to the window, but something seemed to bind his arms and legs. He strained with all his might to break his chains, but in vain. The knocking at the window grew louder and louder. At last the chains broke and Ivan leapt up from the sofa. He looked wildly around him. Both candles had almost burned out, the glass he had just thrown at his visitor stood before him on the table, and there was no one on the sofa opposite. The knocking on the window frame went on insistently, but it was by no means as loud as it had seemed in his dream. On the contrary, it was quite soft.
“It was not a dream! No, I swear it was not a dream, it all happened just now!” cried Ivan. He rushed to the window and opened the small hinged pane.
“Alyosha, I told you not to come,” he cried fiercely to his brother. “In two words, what do you want? In two words, do you hear?”
“An hour ago Smerdyakov hanged himself,” Alyosha answered from the yard.
“Come round to the steps, I’ll open at once,” said Ivan, going to open the door to Alyosha.
